questions.question: What is semantic versioning?
questions.title: Semantic Versioning
questions.direct_answer: SemVer is a version scheme MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g. 2.4.1): increment MAJOR for a breaking change (an API that's no longer compatible), MINOR for a new backward-compatible feature, PATCH for a backward-compatible bug fix. The promise: a user can update to a higher MINOR or PATCH safely (no breakage), but a MAJOR bump means they must check for breaking changes. Bundler's '~> 2.4' (>= 2.4, < 3.0) trusts this — it allows MINOR/PATCH updates but blocks a MAJOR. Knowing SemVer tells you when a gem update is safe (same MAJOR) and when to read the changelog (MAJOR bumped).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH and what triggers each bump (breaking/feature/bugfix) and that '~> 2.4' trusts it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating every version bump as risky (MINOR/PATCH should be safe), or bumping MAJOR for a small change (reserve it for breaking changes).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: SemVer = MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR: breaking change; MINOR: new feature (compatible); PATCH: bug fix. '~> 2.4' allows MINOR/PATCH, blocks MAJOR.

sections.title: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
sections.content: SemVer is a version scheme MAJOR dot MINOR dot PATCH, like 2.4.1: increment MAJOR for a breaking change — an API that's no longer compatible; MINOR for a new backward-compatible feature; PATCH for a backward-compatible bug fix. The promise: a user can update to a higher MINOR or PATCH safely, with no breakage, but a MAJOR bump means they must check for breaking changes. Bundler's tilde-greater 2.4 (greater-than-or-equal 2.4, less than 3.0) trusts this — it allows MINOR and PATCH updates but blocks a MAJOR. Knowing SemVer tells you when a gem update is safe (same MAJOR) and when to read the changelog (a MAJOR bumped).

sections.title: Version Numbers
sections.content:
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; each part has a meaning.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[MAJOR: breaking change] --> Mi[MINOR: new feature, compatible]
  Mi --> P[PATCH: bug fix, compatible]
```

sections.title: SemVer
sections.content:
```ruby
# A version: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, e.g. 2.4.1
#   2  -> MAJOR (breaking change)
#   4  -> MINOR (new backward-compatible feature)
#   1  -> PATCH (backward-compatible bug fix)

# Examples of bumps:
#   1.0.0 -> 2.0.0   # MAJOR: renamed/removed an API (breaking!)
#   1.4.0 -> 1.5.0   # MINOR: added a new method (safe to update)
#   1.4.0 -> 1.4.1   # PATCH: fixed a bug (safe to update)

# Bundler's '~>' trusts SemVer:
gem 'rails', '~> 7.0'    # >= 7.0, < 8.0 (allows 7.x, blocks 8.0 breaking)
gem 'pg', '~> 1.4.1'     # >= 1.4.1, < 1.5 (allows 1.4.x patches)

# Same MAJOR = safe to update; new MAJOR = read the changelog.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Treating every bump as risky — MINOR/PATCH should be safe (read the changelog for MAJOR).
Bumping MAJOR for a small change — reserve it for actual breaking changes.
Forgetting that '~> 2.4' allows MINOR/PATCH but blocks MAJOR (that's the point).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: MAJOR: a breaking change; MINOR: a new backward-compatible feature; PATCH: a backward-compatible bug fix.
Same MAJOR = safe to update; a MAJOR bump = read the changelog for breaking changes.
Bundler's '~> 2.4' (>= 2.4, < 3.0) trusts SemVer: allows MINOR/PATCH, blocks MAJOR.
Reserve MAJOR for real breaking changes; don't bump it for a small feature.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: SemVer is a version scheme MAJOR dot MINOR dot PATCH, like 2.4.1: increment MAJOR for a breaking change — an API that's no longer compatible; MINOR for a new backward-compatible feature; PATCH for a backward-compatible bug fix. The promise: a user can update to a higher MINOR or PATCH safely, with no breakage, but a MAJOR bump means they must check for breaking changes. Bundler's tilde-greater 2.4 (greater-than-or-equal 2.4, less than 3.0) trusts this — it allows MINOR and PATCH updates but blocks a MAJOR. Knowing SemVer tells you when a gem update is safe, same MAJOR, and when to read the changelog, when a MAJOR bumped. A common mistake is treating every version bump as risky, when MINOR and PATCH should be safe, and bumping MAJOR for a small change, when you should reserve it for breaking changes.
